q: A prompt has 3k system, 5k tools, 60k history and 25k retrieval in a 100k window, with max output 20k. What is the issue?
options: Total input fits, but input plus reserved output is 113k
The output reservation is fine since it is billed separately
Retrieval should always be larger than history
Nothing, since it is under 100k of input
why: Input is 93k and reserving 20k output exceeds 100k. Window limits cover input plus output; the last option ignores the output share.

q: Accuracy falls as you pack more passages though everything fits. Best explanation?
options: Context rot: distractors and diluted attention
why: Longer context can degrade use of relevant facts. Tokenizer error would cause overflow, not subtler accuracy loss.

q: You suspect lost-in-the-middle. Which experiment is most diagnostic?
options: Vary the position of the same key fact across the prompt and compare accuracy
Switch to a larger model without measuring
why: Position sweeps isolate the effect. Others change confounders.

q: An agent drops its safety rules after long sessions. What is the most likely first check?
options: Whether the rendered final prompt still contains the rules or truncated them
why: Blind front truncation commonly deletes system text. Inspect the rendered request first.

q: Where should a tiny rule that applies on every call live?
options: Always present in the stable prefix
Only in the last user turn history
why: Small and universal rules stay resident. Retrieval can miss them, which is costly.

q: You must fit 10 candidate passages into room for 4. Best policy?
options: Pick by relevance per token, keep mandatory items, cap per source
why: Score-per-cost selection with protected items maximises value. First-four ignores reranking and length.

q: What is the main benefit of labelling blocks by source?
options: It removes the need for retrieval
It supports attribution and separates untrusted data from instructions
why: Labels help citations and injection defence. They do not reduce tokens.

q: A tool returned file v1, then you edited it to v2, and both are in history. Risk?
options: Stale v1 may be acted on, so keep only the latest
None, models always prefer later text
why: Models can rely on the outdated copy. Replace by key, not just by order.

q: Which ordering is sound for a long prompt?
options: Stable rules, labelled references, history, current request last
why: Stable rules first helps caching and clarity; the request last keeps it in the strong end position.

q: Which summary best supports resuming a debugging session?
options: The user asked about an error
Goal, hypotheses tried, current cause suspected, exact failing test and next step
why: Resumption needs goal, state, failures and ids. The others lose actionable detail.

q: A 30k-token log was read once and the agent only needs the conclusion. Best action?
options: Replace with a concise result and a reference to the stored full log
Summarise it generically with no pointer
why: Reversible compaction keeps access. Deleting loses recoverability; a pointer-less summary may omit needed details.

q: What is the main risk of summarising summaries repeatedly?
options: Cumulative drift and loss of details
why: Each pass is lossy. Prefer summarising from raw segments.

q: Which data should never be paraphrased in a summary?
options: The order ids, paths and numbers needed later
why: Exact values are used programmatically and must be preserved verbatim.

q: Which compression is safest if future needs are uncertain?
options: Offload raw data externally and keep a pointer
why: Reversible reduction retains the ability to recover details.

q: Where should a long task's plan live so it survives context resets?
options: In a durable file re-read at the start of each window
why: A file is exact and persistent. Old messages get summarised or truncated.

q: Active context is best compared to:
why: Active context is the working set; stored context is paged in as needed.

q: An agent never uses its memory store though it holds useful facts. Most likely cause?
options: No index or instruction exposes what is stored
why: Discoverability is required for paging in.

q: Why verify a stored note about a running service before acting?
options: Volatile facts can change after the note was written
why: Notes can go stale; verify live state for volatile facts.

q: When is it safe to remove a large tool result from context?
options: After its needed content is recorded elsewhere or retrievable
Only at the end of a project
why: Free after storing or confirming it is not needed.

q: Which statement about a 1M-token window is most accurate?
options: It raises capacity but not necessarily accuracy, cost or speed
It eliminates the need for retrieval
why: Capacity differs from quality and cost. Retrieval still helps.

q: For summarising an entire short book, which approach fits best?
options: Stuff or map-reduce over the whole text
why: Global tasks need full coverage, unlike pointed lookups where retrieval wins.

q: Retrieved passages are all present, but the model misses the one in the middle. Best first move?
options: Rerank, reduce the number and place the best at the edges
why: Position and noise are the issue; more passages worsen it.

q: Retrieval's characteristic failure is:
options: Using more tokens than the corpus
why: If the retriever misses a chunk, the model never sees it.

q: An ablation shows removing a 5k-token block leaves accuracy unchanged. What do you do?
options: Drop or shrink it, as it costs tokens without value
why: Ablation reveals useless context; remove it.

q: Why does adding 40 more tools to an agent raise cost even if they are never called?
options: Their schemas are sent with every request
Schemas are sent once per session
why: Definitions occupy input tokens on every call and can also hurt selection.

q: A good tool-output design returns:
options: What the model needs, with limits and a way to fetch more
why: Filtered, paginated output with a path to more keeps context lean without blocking access.

q: Where should you aggregate a large dataset for a count question?
options: In the model's reasoning over pasted rows
In the tool or a query, returning the count
why: Deterministic aggregation is exact and cheap.

q: Which approach reduces observation build-up while preserving recoverability?
options: Replace old payloads with placeholders pointing to stored results
why: Placeholders plus external storage keep information recoverable.

q: Swapping the tool list every turn may hurt because:
options: It can invalidate the cached prompt prefix
why: Cache prefixes depend on identical leading content.

q: Prompt caching matches which part of the request?
why: Caches are keyed on the exact leading tokens, so order matters.

q: Where should the current date go to preserve cache hits?
options: First line of the system prompt
In the dynamic part near the end
why: A changing value early invalidates everything after it.

q: Per-turn cost is dominated by the repeated 25k static prefix. Best fix?
options: Cache the prefix and keep it stable
why: Caching cuts repeated cost; shuffling breaks hits.

q: A cache dashboard shows low hit rate only for one template version. First step?
options: Diff the prefixes between requests of that version
why: Prefix diffs reveal volatile content.

q: Which cut is likely best value?
why: Cut the largest low-value block first, then evaluate.

q: Which best describes an agent harness?
options: Code around the model: loop, tools, context, memory, guardrails
why: The harness is the controllable system that wraps the model.

q: The trace shows the needed file was never given to the model. This is:
options: A harness problem to fix by supplying the information
why: Missing context is a harness issue, not a capability limit.

q: Which rule should be enforced in code rather than the prompt?
options: Never delete files outside the project directory
why: Destructive constraints need deterministic guards.

q: A new context window starts for a long project. What should happen first?
options: Read the progress file and repository state to orient
why: Handoff artifacts are the memory; read them first.

q: Why keep test definitions out of the agent's edit permissions?
options: The agent could weaken tests to appear successful
why: Protecting checks prevents gaming.

q: A sub-agent is best used when:
options: Edits are tightly coupled in one file
Exploration is noisy and can return a condensed result
why: Isolation pays off for broad, noisy or parallel work.

q: Which provides the strongest feedback loop for a web feature?
options: Running the app and end-to-end checks and reading results
why: Real execution gives deterministic signals.

q: A turn is over budget. Which overflow action is unsafe because it often deletes standing rules?
options: Refuse a single oversized paste and say so
Drop the oldest elastic history after a cap
why: Front truncation commonly removes the system prompt or the original goal. Refuse, compress elastic blocks, or drop oldest elastic history instead.

q: You must defend 8k versus 128k for a product. What evidence belongs in the argument?
options: The brochure maximum for the flagship model
Success, p95 latency, and cost per successful task at both sizes
A single anecdotal ticket that needed a long paste
why: Window size is a measured product choice. Compare quality, latency, and dollars per success; do not default to the advertised maximum.

q: Two equally trusted docs disagree on an SLA. What should the assembler do before the call?
options: Stuff both and hope the model notices
Flag the conflict and require the answer to report it, or refuse until a canonical source is chosen
why: Models blend or invent a compromise. Drop only when one version supersedes the other; otherwise flag or refuse.

q: A newer untrusted forum post contradicts yesterday’s internal policy doc. Which wins?
options: The forum post, because recency always wins
The internal doc; recency does not cross trust tiers
why: Recency compares within a tier or the same document id. Untrusted web does not outrank standing policy on product facts.

q: A compaction quality check should fail when which of these is true?
options: The digest is shorter than the raw turns
The summariser says it feels complete
A gold-list goal, id, or open question is no longer findable
Token count fell by more than 30 percent
why: The gate is a deterministic gold list, not token savings or the summariser grading itself.

q: Which turn should stay verbatim even when the window is tight?
options: A three-line approval that states “approved $1200 on PO-88”
An already-noted dead-end error from ten turns ago
why: Short high-stakes text (approvals, prices, ids) is cheap to keep and expensive to paraphrase. Fold the chatter, not the decision.

q: You migrated off Redis but the agent still writes Redis config. What memory bug is most likely?
options: The old fact is still active; it was appended, not superseded
why: Append-only memory returns both facts. Mark the old row superseded on the same entity key and retrieve active rows only.

q: What does the pointer-not-payload rule say after reading a 200-line file?
options: Paste the file so it stays available
Delete any record of the read
Keep only the file name with no claim
Keep path plus a one-line claim; re-read when you need bytes
why: Chat copies go stale on the next edit. A path and a specific claim tell you whether to re-read.

q: A needle-placement sweep is most useful when the needle is:
options: A unique UUID the model can spot without reading nearby text
A required constraint the answer must obey, moved through many offsets
A different fact at every offset
The entire document pasted at each offset
why: A constraint sweep shows where obedience breaks. Easy unique strings and changing facts confound the curve.

q: When is a bigger window actually worth paying for?
options: Whenever the model brochure lists a larger number
For every greeting, to be safe
When retrieval cannot reconstruct the needed span and an eval beats the baseline enough to justify cost
When you have not tried chunking yet
why: Pointed questions stay on retrieve. Long context is an exception you prove against a retrieve-or-summarise baseline.

q: A tool-loop observation cap should keep which of these even after old payloads are dropped?
options: The full stdout of every past tool
Nothing; wipe the action log too
A placeholder with the conclusion and a store id, plus the compact action log
Only the tool names with no results
why: Clearing conclusions causes repeat calls. Keep a one-line result and an id; cap the raw payloads.

q: Dynamic tool menus should change when:
options: The task phase changes, then stay stable so the prefix can cache
The model asks for a random tool
why: Per-turn swaps bust the cache and confuse the model. Flip at phase boundaries and reject off-menu calls.

q: A cache breakpoint is useful only if you also:
options: Put timestamps and request ids after it, never before
Put a unique nonce in the system prompt
Keep the breakpoint a secret from CI
why: The prefix before the fence must be byte-identical. Volatile ids and dates belong after it.

q: Which content must stay out of the stable cached prefix?
options: House rules shared by every user
Public tool schemas that rarely change
Secrets, per-user personal data, and one-off tool results
A versioned product manual used on most calls
why: Caching is reuse. Secrets and PII increase blast radius; one-off dumps are not a shared-stable prefix.

q: After a window reset, what should the new session treat as the working window?
options: The model’s memory of the last plan
A newly invented plan to be safe
The progress file plus git and test artefacts
why: The progress file is what survives. Chat may be gone or stale; boot by re-reading artifacts.

q: A parent pastes its full history into every sub-agent “for context.” What did it lose?
options: Nothing; more context is always better
Isolation: the child is as large and noisy as the parent, and you pay twice
why: A contract allowlists what the child may see and size-caps what it returns. Pasting the parent transcript voids isolation.
